We expect smaller fundamental surpluses from 2011 and much less pronounced Russian official stockpile sales. High marginal PGM production costs, a tightening physical market and investmentrelated demand for hard assets should support the price. We now see room for prices to be approaching $500/oz in real terms by the end of our forecast period. And there may be further upside potential if the growth of petrol vehicles fitted with emissions after-treatment systems proves stronger than we expect and/or there is more rapid substitution of palladium for platinum and even rhodium in automotive after-treatment applications. Even without this, we expect the platinum:palladium price r

atio to fall towards the levels of the early 2000s over our forecast period. 

After bouncing this year, the delayed response of jewellery manufacturers to already higher prices could dampen total consumption growth in 2011.  But 2012 should then see the start of a longer-lasting upturn even if palladium continues to under-perform in Western markets.  We expect the automotive sector to remain the major source of palladium demand.  And there will be very strong production growth of light duty petrol fuelled vehicles fitted with palladium rich autocatalyst devices in developing economies.  Palladium loadings on diesel (and petrol) emissions after-treatment systems will also rise as higher quality fuels become more widely available.  Developing populous economies such as India and China will therefore account for an increasing proportion of global offtake. 

Delayed investment means miners will struggle to meet this increase in industrial consumption.  Higher PGM prices into 2010 have led to less challenging capital financing conditions for PGM producers.  But increased regulatory focus since the start of the year on reducing trading liquidity in financial and commodity markets and raising banks’ capital reserves suggest producers’ ability to access external funding may be constrained for longer than we had previously thought – to now beyond 2010.  So producers will continue to prioritise cost management and optimisation of existing mining operations, and capital expenditure plans will remain subject to review.  Meanwhile, in South Africa, we do not expect platinum prices to comfortably exceed the estimated marginal cost of production on a sustained basis over our forecast period, and this will hold back associated by-product palladium supply.  And uncertainty regarding the application of Zimbabwe’s BEE legislation will make companies more cautious about investing there, although it is not clear the extent to which these investments will be directed to other regions.

#### Other precious metal markets 

###### Gold 

We still take the view that re-monetisation of gold, at the national and international level, will be a dominant driver of the gold price, despite the recent change in market psychology favouring the US dollar. 



- Taking account of the pull-back in the gold price from over $1,200/oz in early December 2009, we have lowered our 2010 Q1-Q3 forecasts, but have kept our 2011-14 price outlook unchanged for the time being.  We still expect nominal gold prices to remain mostly above $1,100/oz. 



- Whether or not gold is included in any recomposed IMF SDR basket in late 2010 (it could be deferred to the next review in 2015) will set the scene for what subsequently happens to the gold price. 



- The sharp rise in bullion prices and producer margins has led to an increase in actual and potential mine supply, but longer-term gold mine supply

remains constrained. ###### Silver Our latest tabulations confirm that the market’s surplus swelled to the equivalent of 20% of fabrication demand in 2009. Even with offtake recovering strongly through to 2014, production restraint is needed if a more balanced market is to develop. And this needs lower prices. - Mine production is estimated to have increased by 1,050 tonnes in 2009, and further growth could result in market surpluses of a similar magnitude continuing through to 2014 if silver’s price does not fall towards $8/oz before then. - Even outside China, economic recovery is now lifting fabrication demand. ###### Platinum We still expect the platinum market to return to a period of sustained deficits from 2011. - This tightening of the physical market combined with high marginal production costs and continued investment-related demand for hard assets should support the price. We have raised our forecasts to average around $1,490/oz in real terms over 2010-14. - Institutional and high net worth individuals could have a far greater influence on price and metal availability than in the past. But we still expect liquidation of platinum ETF holdings to be stickier than that of previously held asset classes. - Northam Platinum has begun an early works programme to construct roads, pipelines and infrastructure facilities for its greenfield Booysendal mine, with Phase 1 construction goahead likely in July 2010 and first production in 2011. Meanwhile, Eastern Platinum has restarted the development of the Crocette Section of its Crocodile River plant, which had been put on hold in December 2008. ational|480|490| ###### **Note on sources and definitions** Although many of the statistics used in this analysis are taken from _Johnson Matthey_ , there are some important differences between the ways in which we each use these to explain market events. On the **demand** side, _Johnson Matthey’s_ figures generally show net consumption in each end-use, that is the difference between purchases and the amount of metal recovered from old scrap. In contrast, we prefer to list demand gross, and treat the metal recovered from the recycling of end-of-life products as an additional element of supply. In terms of the historical balance, this of course has no effect, since our higher gross consumption is offset one-for-one by higher secondary supply. However, because (a) we feel that economic and other developments drive demand at the gross level and (b) we feel that scrap recovery is driven mainly by consumption in some prior period, this different approach does yield different results when projecting net metal use forward. On the **supply** side, whilst _Johnson Matthey_ generally defines primary output as metal sales by platinum producers, we have meanwhile built our series on the basis of recoverable output mine-by-mine. Through time, these two should of course be the same. And _Johnson Matthey’s_ approach is arguably better for assessing the historical balance year-by-year. However, our choice is again driven by considerations of the future, it being far easier to forecast production on a mine-by-mine basis than at the level of smelters‟ and refineries‟ metal sales. Finally, when looking at the **supply-demand balance** , we refuse to treat bar hoarding or ETFs as part of consumption. Instead, we see these as just another way in which investors hold excess stock, there being no difference between this identifiable material and the other inventories that are implied by the past imbalance between supply and demand. Stockholders will not maintain or build their positions unless they feel that this offers them some economic benefit. And this is just as true of “investors” as it is of any other market participant. Bars and ETFs may be a little less liquid than other surplus metal but, if stockholders‟ mood changes, all previously accumulated metal will be a potential source of additional supply. CRU International Limited confidential Precious Metals Quarterly 2010 Q1 Palladium 9 #### 2. Gross fabrication demand ###### 2.1 Summary We estim

ate that palladium fabrication fell by around 1.1 Moz in 2009 to just below 7.75 Moz. Production declines and destocking were a recurrent theme across palladium‟s industrial end-uses as companies sought to raise funds due to frozen credit lines. This effect was particularly marked for the autocatalyst sector which we estimate took 22% (970 koz) less palladium than in 2008. Across the other industrial end-use segments, palladium offtake suffered a lot less, but may still have slipped by 2% (80 koz) year-on-year. Meanwhile, we believe that the jewellery sector took 5% (45 koz) less palladium on a net basis in 2009 than in 2008, reflecting developments in China where retailers and wholesalers shifted their focus to platinum jewellery to take advantage of relatively low and stable local metal prices, a reduced price differential between gold and platinum, and rising profit margins on platinum pieces on an absolute and relative basis to other metals. From 2010, we expect offtake from autocatalyst and industrial markets to improve. Even though 2008 vehicle production levels in the EU, USA and Japan are unlikely to be regained before 2012, we expect strong production growth in developing economies of light duty petrol fuelled vehicles fitted with autocatalyst devices. Coupled with palladium‟s increased loadings on emissions after-treatment systems for diesel vehicles as ultra low sulphur content diesel fuel becomes more widely available, this should contribute to a more than 75% jump in autocatalystrelated palladium offtake from 2009 levels to 6,185 koz in 2014. Despite their high cost, there has been little outright substitution of PGMs by non-PGM materials due to their excellent catalytic properties for both oxidation and reduction reactions. Also, PGM materials are better able to function throughout the engine temperature cycle without being significantly deactivated through thermal degradation or by poisoning as impurities accumulate on the catalyst‟s surface. 

To comply with legislative changes, automakers innovate with respect to the design of the vehicle engine and associated exhaust gas after-treatment systems.  There have been changes in the quantities of platinum, palladium and rhodium used in the exhaust after-treatment systems and the ratio in which they are applied depending on the type of engine technology adopted.  As a result, aggregate (and individual) PGM content in vehicle exhaust after-treatment systems can vary greatly from one vehicle to another depending on the vehicle design (size and engine type), its target regional sales market, the fuel quality used in that market, and when the model was introduced.  And a trend to smaller vehicles (with reduced engine size and lower associated PGM content) can even offset the higher PGM impact of tighter legislative standards.  Typical aggregate PGM loadings vary from 1.5g to 12g per vehicle, with an average of around 3.1g or lower for a passenger vehicle.  The exact amount and relative PGM loadings for a given vehicle model is usually kept confidential between the catalyst manufacturer and the vehicle manufacturer. 

A conventional (spark ignition) petrol engine vehicle has been able to comply with legislative standards using a single palladium-rich 3-way autocatalyst device to treat exhaust gas emissions.  The 3-way autocatalyst simultaneously converts more than 90% of CO, HCs and NOx produced during the combustion of fuel in the engine into CO2, H2O and N2 in oxidation/ reduction reactions.  NOx conversion is possible because the exhaust gas has a low oxygen content.  The autocatalyst decreases the mass of PM emissions by oxidising some of the hydrocarbons that are absorbed onto the carbon particulates.  Although palladium is not as efficient a catalyst as platinum, petrol-engine catalytic converters are still able to contain palladium-rich loadings allowing vehicle emission limits to meet legislated standards.  And, as a result of price-related substitution, these device loadings now favour palladium with a palladium-to-platinum ratio of 90:10 maximum in markets where low sulphur content petrol is available.  The ratio will be lower in markets where high sulphur content petrol still dominates<sup>4</sup> . Although petrol engine 3-way autocatalyst PGM loadings are palladium rich, actual palladium content has been declining as manufacturers reduce the size of autocatalyst devices in line with the trend for reduced engine size and smaller vehicles.

Even where recycled metal is moving in a closed circuit between manufacturer, end-user and refiner, scrap returns do not necessarily equate to new purchases one-for-one (if they did, there would be no net demand). In addition, the palladium dispersed in spent autocatalysts and in old electronic circuits finds its way via the normal scrap network back to precious metals refiners. Most areas of the secondary palladium network reached maturity many years ago, with a high proportion of all available arisings already being recovered. Future tonnage recycling in these areas will thus continue to be driven just by consumption at various points in the past. And, so as long as there were no step changes in the historical demand trend, future recycling will continue along what are now well-established

paths. Over our forecast period, the key source of palladium scrap will be from spent autocatalysts. The average passenger car has a life of 13-15 years. So our forecast period of 2010-14 will continue to see the scrapping of vehicles mostly produced in the second half of the 1990s. Although vehicles being scrapped in the USA and Japan are already much more likely to contain a catalyst than not, the same is only now becoming true in Western Europe, where catalytic converters only began to be fitted increasingly to vehicles in the second half of the 1990s, with the introduction of Euro 2 in 1997. Furthermore, autocatalysts in the late 1990s contained much higher palladium loadings than currently used in those fitted to smaller, more fuel efficient vehicles. We therefore expect the pool of potentially available material to take a step up in the next five years, while recovery of PGMs from spent catalytic converters in more mature markets will increase – encouraged by a more reliable scrap supply collection chain resulting from tighter recycling legislation (under which the manufacturer is responsible for collection of the scrap vehicle). We expect palladium recovery from autocatalysts to rise much more quickly in the next 5 years and indeed to rise by 1.1 Moz between 2010 and 2014. This will be the major factor behind a 40% growth in total secondary palladium supply over this period. The severity of the economic downturn in 2009 led some consumers to defer scrapping of older vehicles (reducing the number of autocatalysts available for recycling), while lower prices may have discouraged treatment of the spent autocatalysts. Consequently we estimate palladium recovery from spent autocatalysts in 2009 recorded its smallest annual increase in percentage terms this decade. Palladium recovery could have been considerably worse, had it not been for the success of vehicle old-for-new scrappage schemes in 2009; the US and German schemes are estimated to have captured at least 3 million older cars. However, many of these schemes have now expired, which suggests that weak vehicle sales in the short term could be matched by fewer old vehicles scrapped. #### 4.  Mine Production 

###### 4.1  Summary 

Unlike platinum, more than half of all palladium mined today is derived from deposits located outside South Africa.  Last year, South Africa accounted for just under 40% of global palladium mine production compared with a 75% market share for platinum.  Although the Bushveld and Stillwater complexes typically contain much higher concentrations of PGMs than the deposits of the Norilsk-Talnakh and Sudbury regions, the sheer size of the latter base metal sulphides means that their by-product PGM output can still be significant.  And the concentration of palladium is 2-2.5 times higher than platinum in Norilsk-Talnakh ores.  Thus curtailments to South African production are less effective in balancing the palladium than the platinum market, while changes to North American and Russian production have a proportionately greater impact on the palladium market than on that for platinum.  Nonetheless, a firm platinum price is still needed to encourage global PGM and therefore palladium production. 

Following annual declines of 4% in 2007 and 8% in 2008, we estimate that world palladium mine production slipped by a further 4% in 2009 to just under 6.35 Moz.  This pushed output almost 15% below its 2006 high and to its lowest level since the early 2000s.  Canada suffered the greatest year-on-year fall in 2009, both in percentage terms (nearly 50%) and in absolute terms (over 280 koz), due to the suspension of North American Palladium‟s Lac des Iles mine and industrial action at Vale Inco‟s Sudbury operations. 

The slump in metal prices in

the second half of 2008 to below the cash cost of production for a number of PGM producers, forced many in 2009 to embark on a strategy of closing high cost operations, significantly reducing headcount, optimising existing operations and improving productivity. Majors (including Impala Platinum, Anglo Platinum and Lonmin) and junior miners scaled back project capex and stay-in-business capital investment plans, particularly for projects with long lead times. Planned progress in reducing unit costs was hindered by unexpected production disruptions such as industrial action in Canada (Vale Inco‟s Sudbury) and South Africa (Impala Platinum‟s Impala Lease) and Section 54 safety-related stoppages in South Africa (particularly at Impala Platinum and Lonmin). And operations and projects which had been placed on care and maintenance in 2008 remained suspended throughout 2009. The rebound in nickel, copper and PGM prices as global economic conditions stabilised in the second half of 2009, eased cutback pressures for existing PGM operations, and led to announcements towards the end of the year that some suspended operations (Lac des Iles in Canada and Aquarius Platinum‟s Everest in South Africa) would re-open in 2010. Higher PGM prices into 2010 amid strong interest in PGM investment vehicles42 , and a stabilisation of nickel prices, has led to less challenging financing conditions for PGM producers since 2009 Q4. Share placements are being conducted to repay long-term debt43 . Debt financing for mine projects is now more easily available, even though companies are being required to hedge part of their forward production to protect their initial income stream. Market balance and prices In our view, six elements combine to determine the palladium price. The first is industrial dem

and in autocatalysts and other applications.  Although there is some price elasticity here as platinum‟s value fluctuates vis-а-vis those of other PGMs, the main drivers of industrial demand are economic activity and environmental legislation.  The second element is the scrap supply which arises from the recycling of old industrial goods.  Again, although people engaged in the secondary industry may choose to hold or release stocks in response to changes in price, this supply is driven mainly by consumption at various points in the past.  Miners aim to fill the gap between gross demand and secondary supply.  However, the lead time to develop additional mine capacity can often be substantial, so it is hard for them to react quickly to market shortages and higher prices.  The fourth element of the market is instead the most price-sensitive.  This is jewellery demand.  As the margin of supply over other consumption narrows, prices rise and jewellery manufacturers get squeezed.  Conversely, when supply moves significantly above other demand, jewellery offtake gets a boost from the lower prices that result.  But this bidding of metal to and from the jewellery sector can be balanced or exacerbated by the accumulation or release of the fifth element in the market, investment stocks.  The final element influencing developments is the sale to the West of palladium stocks previously accumulated by the Russian state. 

During the 1990s and until 2002, the palladium market was mostly in considerable fundamental deficit.  But when adjusted for US DLA<sup>69</sup> and, more particularly, Russian stock changes, we estimate metal availability was considerably enhanced.  During the 1990s and early 2000s, net Russian exports were persistently higher than our estimate of its mine supply, often exceeding output by a very large margin. Since our December _Update_ , there has been a change in market psychology, favouring the US dollar.  Economic data releases suggest that the USA is in a sustainable, albeit slow, recovery.  The Federal Reserve has raised its discount rate for the first time since June 2006. There have been concerns over the ability of a number of euro-zone countries to address their worsening fiscal position without recourse to supranational funding or default.  Emerging market economies (particularly China and India) have begun curbing bank lending growth and are close to raising official rates, as the policy focus shifts from supporting demand to containing price pressures.  In addition, US and European policymakers have proposed curbs on bank proprietary trading activities, tighter regulation of OTC derivative markets, a rise in bank capital reserves and position limits on exchange traded metals derivatives (specifically for gold, silver and copper) which suggests an increased focus on reducing trading liquidity. And this growth is not just to the extent that last year’s losses are recovered. We expect offtake in 2014 to be running up to 8% higher than its pre-recession level of early 2008. Having fallen by 18% between its January 2008 high and its March 2009 low, OECD industrial production had recovered by 6-6.5% by the end of December. And more recent figures for a number of countries point to this upturn having continued in 2010 Q1. We should also remember that these data only cover the most developed Western economies. Chinese econ

s||| Precious Metals Quarterly 2010 Q1 # Chapter 4 Platinum #### Price forecasts raised Platinum prices briefly reached $1,627/oz (PM-fix) on 20 January before retreating to $1,475/oz on 5 February and then recovering to the $1,550-1,575/oz range. So quotations have been volatile in the early part of this year. However, platinum continues to underperform palladium in price terms. Since our December _Focus_ , there has been a change in market psychology favouring the US dollar, such that leveraged speculative long positions, particularly those financed by the US dollar carry trade, have been scaled back. Nonetheless, we still expect investment demand for hard assets to be a price support, reflecting a delay to conventional monetary tightening, an associated delay in normalisation of interest rate differentials, greater official tolerance for inflation in developed economies and a greater geographical spread of investment vehicles backed by physical metal1 . Conditions for producers have brightened since last quarter amid higher PGM prices. Producers are facing less challenging capital market financing conditions; share placements are being conducted to repay long-term debt while debt financing for mine projects is now more easily available, though conditional on hedgi

ng.  And a more stable rand-US dollar exchange rate means that South African producers have been able to capture more of the benefit of higher US dollar PGM prices than previously. 

However, we still do not expect platinum prices to comfortably exceed the estimated marginal cost of production on a sustained basis over our forecast period.  Increased regulatory focus since the start of the year on reducing trading liquidity in financial and commodity markets and on raising banks’ capital reserves suggest producers’ ability to access external funding may be constrained for longer than we had previously thought (ie. now to beyond 2010).  So capital expenditure plans will remain subject to review over an extended time horizon.  In South Africa, which accounts for around three quarters of global platinum mine supply, we expect producers to maintain their emphasis on cost and cash-flow management for longer in order to strengthen balance sheets.

South African producers continue to face a challenging environment what with power constraints, potential labour disputes, upward cost pressures from higher electricity prices and wages, greater mining depths and continued calls for nationalisation of gold and platinum mines.  The 5-year review of the 2004 Mining Charter will become public in 2010 Q1 and is expected to address Black Economic Empowerment progress in all aspects of the mining industry (not just ownership), and the often complex financing deals and ownership structures which enable BEE companies to invest and take an operating role in the mining assets of nonBEE companies.  From 1 May 2010, under the new Mining and Petroleum Royalties Act, producers will be required to pay a royalty tax, regardless of profitability, for unrefined and refined minerals based on their gross sales.  Consequently there should be continued focus on improving productivity and managing the supply chain and procurement costs.  This suggests that new greenfield or brownfield projects will not be easily fast-tracked to production, particularly those with a long time frame.  We therefore continue to expect only a modest recovery in mine supply between 2010 and 2014, although producer cost-cutting strategies should eventually give way to growth strategies over our forecast period.  Expansion projects committed to come on line remain on track, and newer operations are expected to contribute to increased output as they ramp up to steady state production.  Note, we are assuming that the mining sector will be subject to considerably less onerous ownership limits under Zimbabwe’s new BEE legislation.  If this prov

es not to be the case, producers may divert planned investments from PGM interests in Zimbabwe to other regions, which could help the development of some South African projects. Miners will find it difficult to meet a rise in net fabrication demand, which will be supported by increasing momentum in the automotive and industrial sectors from 2011-12 as the world economy turns. The heavy duty diesel sector for on-road and non-road vehicles and engines will offer significant expansion opportunities for platinum-rich after-treatment systems, as will the increased take-up of fuel efficient light duty diesel and hybrid vehicles in mature markets despite reduced platinum loadings relative to palladium on diesel vehicle types. In the jewellery sector, China should remain a key and growing platinum market. Ahead of the Chinese New Year holiday period, the volume of 99.95% purity platinum being bought through the Shanghai Gold Exchange has already been robust. We therefore expect the physical market to return to a period of sustained deficits from 2011 before approaching a more finely balanced market towards the end of our forecast period. High marginal PGM production costs, a tightening physical market and investment-related demand for hard assets should support the price, and we have raised our forecasts since our December _Focus_ to average around $1,490/oz in real terms. Policy to become more of a brake The outlook has improved a little, thanks to Asia, but the recovery in the developed world remains fragile and shallow, chiefly because it’s rooted narrowly in trade, the stock cycle and policy measures. Thus the spill over effects from China’s vigorous upturn should benefit global prospects in the short-term. In the medium term, however, as that support eases, and the developed world becomes more dependent on underlying domestic demand, its ability to grow will be constrained by fiscal retrenchment as well as structural adjustments arising from savings behaviour, demand rebalancing and demographics. The fallout from Greece’s fiscal crisis, which has been building over the past month, has turned the spotlight on fiscal imbalances across the developed world, almost all of which are deteriorating substantially in the wake of the rescues mounted in 2008 and 2009. The heightened risk of defaults on sovereign debt has led financial markets to demand significantly greater risk premiums in some cases. Unless policy makers map out convincing plans to return their budget deficits to sustainable levels, and to timetables the markets deem reasonable, the cost of borrowing across much of the developed world will rise, damaging growth. The run up in yields on higher risk sovereign bonds is already affecting parts of the corporate debt market. So once the immediate emergency is over fis

cal austerity is in the offing for a significant number of developed economies.  Thus the timing and pace with which fiscal and monetary stimulus is unwound is the key to the cycle in short term.  But the likely drags resulting from fiscal retrenchment and global demand rebalancing are the keys to the medium term. 



The recovery gathered pace in the fourth quarter, but not universally.  Chinese GDP was up almost 11% year-on-year (y-o-y), compared with 8.8% in the third.  US GDP was up 0.1% y-o-y, or 5.7% quarter-on-quarter (q-o-q) annualised, versus 2.2% in the third.  Japan’s GDP expanded 0.4% y-o-y, or 4.6% q-o-q annualised.   The Eurozone could only manage 0.1% q- o-q, however. 



Amid concerns about overheating, in the labour market as well as asset markets, China tightened policy further in February, albeit moderately.  This reinforces our view that its economy will be cooling in 2011, thereby throwing the developed world back more on domestic demand as the engine of its recovery.

So what’s going to support domestic demand as the initial impetus to recovery from stocks and exports wanes?  The fiscal stimulus will help through the rest of 2010, and into the early months of 2011.  Around 70% of stimulus funds are scheduled to be spent by the end of September 2010.  And the package has been reinforced by further stimulus measures to a total value of $150 billion, focused on employment incentives, and more recently supplemented by a far smaller $15 billion package.   Monetary policy in terms of interest rates applicable to consumer and business lending, meanwhile, will remain very supportive for the next 9-12 months.  True, the Fed has begun the slow process of withdrawing the support it extended to the financial sector in 2008: in mid February it raised its discount rate from 0.5% to 0.75%. ###### 2.2 Europe: Fiscal deficits weigh on outlook 

Aspects of the outlook for Europe are similar to those for the USA, except that the recovery in Europe has got off to a slower, less certain start, and the fiscal prospects are if anything worse.  Growth in the Eurozone decelerated in the fourth quarter as the boost from exports ebbed.  The headlines have been dominated by Greece, however, and its dire public finances – its budget deficit shot up to almost 13% of GDP in 2009 – but large parts of the Eurozone, and the UK, are in almost as much fiscal trouble, and the solutions they will have to implement will weigh every bit as heavily on the outlook as those in the USA, even though private indebtedness is less of a problem. 

The region recorded anaemic growth at the end of 2009.  GDP expanded by only 0.1% quarter-on-quarter in the final three months of 2009, following an advance of 0.4% in the third quarter.  Crucially Germany stagnated.  France recorded the strongest performance, growing by 0.6%.  Activity in Italy and Spain contracted.  Although the detail isn’t available yet the deceleration was probably attributable to an easing in the stock cycle, domestically and overseas.  But Europe is benefiting less from the upt

urn in Asia also, partly because of competitiveness, which may have been partly responsible for the 1.7% month-on-month fall in industrial production in December, and partly because it’s been orientated towards the emerging markets in Central and Eastern Europe, which are recovering slowly compared with Asia. 

Sentiment indicators point to a modest resumption of growth in the short term, which could get a boost from the recent falls in the euro following the rise in sovereign risk.  But the region will struggle nonetheless because with the exception of France domestic demand is stagnant at best, and the prospect of a period of fiscal austerity is unlikely to help.   In Germany the household sector is likely to be very cautious over the next two years because of the prospect of further increases in unemployment as employment subsidies are withdrawn, as nominal wages stagnate and as tax cuts are delayed. #### Tightening slowly extends to developed economies

#### Euro taking a fiscal hit 

In our forecasts short to medium-term parities are influenced by market-making factors, such as comparative interest rates, which are of a cyclical nature, and inflation expectations, trade deficits and relative growth rates, which are of a more structural nature.  Increasingly, however, some of these structural influences may act in opposition to cyclical influences.  For instance, a currency may not weaken much in response to cuts in interest rates that are made mainly to support growth.  In the long term, however, currencies are projected to revert towards their `fair’ values, which are closely akin to the values implied by purchasing power parities.  In other words currencies are forecast to revert to cross-parities that compensate for the varying prices, in local currency terms, of a common basket of goods. 



- The US dollar has tended to benefit from anxieties about sovereign debt, on the one hand, and from evidence of recovery in the USA, especially in its financial sector, on the other. But as soon as worries abate the dollar invariably resumes its depreciation.  Indeed, we expect the dollar to continue to weaken on trend against its key surplus trading partners as part of the rebalancing of the US economy, for several years yet.  In the short term, moreover, there is scope for considerable volatility when policy starts to tighten and dollarbased carry trades are unwound.  However, the dollar’s role as a safe haven and reserve currency suggest that its downside is limited on a broader basis. 



- The euro has weakened to nine-month plus lows of around $1.34-1.35/€ as financial markets have reacted to the Greek fiscal crisis, and a generally riskier environment for the Eurozone as a whole, resulting from similar concerns about other EU economies including Belgium, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and the fear of contagion.  Indeed, some hedge funds are selling the euro forward to the tune of $12 billion, in the expectation that the Eurozone’s internal contradictions will lead to a collapse in the single currency.  The euro was overvalued before the crisis struck, in the aftermath of the Greek

election, so much of this shake-out was warranted on the basis of the underlying weaknesses in the Eurozone economy anyway. Indeed, over the medium term we believe that the euro will continue to weaken on trend to a more sustainable value in the range $1.28-1.30/€.  As a result there is scope for it to over shoot on its way down, before reaching its equilibrium value. 



- The yen strengthened on trend for much of 2009, partly as a result of the recovery in its exports, and partly because of the negative pressures dragging down the US dollar.  But it looks like it’s in urgent need of a bout of weakness to help support Japan’s external sector, prompted to a degree by heightened sensitivity towards its poor public finances.  As a result we have the yen weakening a little in 2010.  From a medium to longer term perspective, however, Japan’s surplus will tend to exert upward pressure which should correct some of the short-term losses. 



- The pound has weakened in the wake of the UK’s lacklustre recovery, its continuing exposure to financial sector risk, deteriorating public finances, which on some measures are comparable with those of Greece, and absence of a credible deficit reduction plan.  It is approaching year lows under $1.50/£.  There are signs that speculators are starting to bet against sterling as well.  A correction, certainly towards $1.60/£, was merited on the basis of the UK’s economic fundamentals.  However, on the assumption that a credible deficit reduction plan is forthcoming the lows that sterling hit during the early months of 2010 look like they exaggerate its underlying weakness.  Thus a modest recovery to a more sustainable value around $1.60-1.63/£ looks probable over the medium term. 



- The Australian dollar has strengthened further as a result of Australia’s robust recovery, and the allied expectation of a series of interest rate rises to come.  Thus it dipped when interest rates weren’t raised as expected in early February.  However, as we’ve argued before, Australia’s persistent current account deficit, which is currently in the range of 5-6% of
